First, the threshold depends on the constant arising from the O⁡(Δ​tp)O({\Delta t}^{p}) term in (24), associated with the RK scheme and commonly depending on the Lipschitz constant of f^\hat{f} and the time horizon TT. Second, the threshold depends on the order of convergence pp of the numerical scheme, which is guaranteed to be attained only if f^\hat{f} is sufficiently regular, hence the requirement on the activation function ϱ\varrho to be Cp​(ℝ)C^{p}(\mathbb{R}).

4 Velocity matching

The stability estimates provided in Section 3 justify replacing the trajectory-based objective with a velocity-based objective, a quadratic functional whose unique minimizer is the true velocity field ff. While avoiding simulation of the learned dynamics, this objective is, however, not directly accessible, as it requires knowledge of the true velocity field along the reference trajectories, not available in practice. Any empirical surrogate of the theoretical velocity objective must therefore rely on velocity estimates as supervision signal from discrete observations of the system state. In this view, this is a price to be paid for removing simulation from training. Here we introduce a principled velocity-based objective, which we call velocity matching. Rather than supervising the learned velocity field f^\hat{f} at the discrete observation points, as in commonly adopted teacher forcing (TF) approaches, VM evaluates f^\hat{f} along the piecewise linear interpolant of the observed trajectories, at times sampled uniformly within each interval, and supervises it with the velocity obtained by differentiating the interpolant.

In the following, in Section 4.1 we introduce the VM objective and describe its algorithmic implementation, framing it as an instance of an interpolant-based surrogate for ℒf\mathcal{L}_{f} and relating it to prior work. Section 4.2 provides a bias-variance decomposition of the VM loss, and relates the VM bias term to the residual of an implicit Runge-Kutta method, highlighting the implicit nature of the resulting update. Section 4.3 interprets VM loss as a stochastic quadrature rule, establishing O⁡(Δ​t2)O({\Delta t}^{2}) order of approximation of the loss associated with the theoretical velocity objective ℒf\mathcal{L}_{f}. Section 4.4 casts VM as a regularized velocity regression whose penalty implicitly matches the action of the Jacobian of the learned velocity field to that of the true velocity field.

4.1 Empirical objective and algorithmic aspects

We seek an empirical counterpart of the theoretical velocity objective ℒf\mathcal{L}_{f}, defined in (10), overcoming the limitation of requiring knowledge of the true velocity field along the reference trajectories. A natural approach, dating back to the early developments of system identification [Bellman and Roth, 1971, Varah, 1982, Ramsay et al., 2007], consists in relying on two-stage estimation, where a prior interpolation step produces a continuous approximation x~​(t,x0)\tilde{x}(t,x_{0}) of the observed trajectories, from which velocities can be estimated by differentiating such an interpolant. Then, the learned vector field f^\hat{f} is matched with the estimated velocities along the interpolated trajectories, yielding a surrogate objective for ℒf\mathcal{L}_{f}, which we denote by ℒ~f,N,Nt\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{f,N,{N_{t}}}, reading as

ℒ~f,N,Nt​[f^]=1N​∑i=1Nℓ~f,Nt​(f^,x0(i)),ℓ~f,Nt​(f^,x0)=1T​‖∂tx~​(⋅,x0)−f^​(⋅,x~​(⋅,x0))‖L2​([0,T],ℝn)2.\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{f,N,{N_{t}}}[\hat{f}]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{\ell}_{f,{N_{t}}}(\hat{f};x_{0}^{(i)}),\quad\tilde{\ell}_{f,{N_{t}}}(\hat{f};x_{0})=\frac{1}{T}\|\partial_{t}\tilde{x}(\cdot,x_{0})-\hat{f}(\cdot,\tilde{x}(\cdot,x_{0}))\|^{2}_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}. (26)

Although built from the finite set of Nt+1{N_{t}}+1 observations, the surrogate objective is expressed in continuous-time form through the L2L^{2}-norm over [0,T][0,T], since the interpolant x~​(⋅,x0)\tilde{x}(\cdot,x_{0}) provides a, possibly almost everywhere, continuous approximation of the observed trajectories and velocities, whose regularity is set by the chosen interpolation strategy. While prior approaches have favored globally regular interpolants, as cubic [Bellman and Roth, 1971] or quintic splines [Hou et al., 2026], we adopt piecewise linear interpolation for the following reasons. First, the L2L^{2} objective is insensitive to the regularity at the knots {tk}k=0Nt\{t_{k}\}_{k=0}^{{N_{t}}}, a set of null measure, so that almost everywhere differentiability of the interpolant suffices to ensure well-posedness of the objective. Second, piecewise linear interpolation carries the computational cost of a first-order finite difference, as opposed to the cost of fitting higher-order splines. Although the resulting supervision signal is now piecewise constant, with discontinuities at the knots, the spectral bias [Rahaman et al., 2019, Xu et al., 2019] of neural network parameterizations of f^\hat{f} allows smoothness to be recovered at the level of the approximator rather than on the target.

This choice yields the velocity matching (VM) objective, denoted by ℒf,N,NtVM\mathcal{L}_{f,N,{N_{t}}}^{\rm{VM}} with per-sample loss ℓf,NtVM\ell_{f,{N_{t}}}^{\rm{VM}}, as the specific instance of the empirical surrogate objective (26) obtained from piecewise linear interpolation of the observed trajectories, with

x~​(t,x0):=x⁡(tk,x0)+(t−tk)​vk​(x0),∂tx~​(t,x0)=vk​(x0):=x⁡(tk+1,x0)−x⁡(tk,x0)tk+1−tk,\tilde{x}(t,x_{0}):=x(t_{k},x_{0})+(t-t_{k})\,v_{k}(x_{0}),\qquad\partial_{t}\tilde{x}(t,x_{0})=v_{k}(x_{0}):=\dfrac{x(t_{k+1},x_{0})-x(t_{k},x_{0})}{t_{k+1}-t_{k}}, (27)

for t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}) and k=0,…,Nt−1k=0,\dots,{N_{t}}-1. Under uniform temporal discretizations, the L2L^{2}-norm in (26) decomposes over subintervals, and sampling the integration variable uniformly within each of them recasts the loss as a stochastic perturbation of the time and space arguments in f^\hat{f}. Accordingly, we define the per-sample VM loss as

which we adopt in practice. Its consistency with the interpolant-based objective is stated below and proved in Appendix C.1.

Formulation (28) unfolds the structure of the VM objective in terms of a stochastic perturbation along the interpolant. Analytically, sampling the offset τ\tau to evaluate the learned vector field f^\hat{f} along the continuum of each subinterval, rather than at its left endpoint alone as in TF, yields: (i) a higher order of approximation of the theoretical velocity objective, and (ii) an implicit regularization effect on the Jacobian of the learned vector field, as shown in Section 4.3 and Section 4.4, respectively. Computationally, it reduces to a sampling procedure mirroring that of flow matching approaches [Lipman et al., 2023, Hou et al., 2026], as discussed in Remark 2. We detail the batched implementation in Algorithm 1. In particular, the triple (ij,kj,τj)(i_{j},k_{j},\tau_{j}) denotes the indices of the jj-th sample in the batch, of size BB, with iji_{j} and kjk_{j} denoting the trajectory and temporal indices, respectively, and τj\tau_{j} the offset within the selected subinterval. The velocity target vjv_{j} is computed as the first-order finite difference approximation of the velocity along the selected trajectory and temporal index, while the collocation point (t~j,x~j)(\tilde{t}_{j},\tilde{x}_{j}) is obtained by advancing along the chord connecting the two consecutive observations, with offset τj\tau_{j}. The learned vector field f^\hat{f} is then evaluated at the collocation point and matched with the velocity target vjv_{j}. Thus, as each step evaluates the learned vector field at a single collocation point per sample, and constructs the velocity target as a first-order finite difference, the computational cost of VM is comparable to that of an explicit Euler TF update. Since the offset τj\tau_{j} is sampled independently across the batch, the batch size BB controls the variance of the resulting gradient estimate.

Remark 2 (Connection to flow matching).

The VM construction is formally a flow matching (FM) objective [Lipman et al., 2023], where a learned velocity field is regressed onto the time derivative of an interpolant joining two endpoint samples, with the velocity field being evaluated along the interpolant itself. The connection with operator learning, in a continuous-time setting, was made explicit by Hou et al. [2026], within the stochastic interpolant framework [Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023, Albergo et al., 2025]. However, VM differs from FM in the coupling between endpoints and, as a result, in the object being learned. Denote by ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) the law of x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}) with x0∼ρ0x_{0}\sim\rho_{0}, and by νk\nu_{k} the joint law of (x⁡(tk,x0),x⁡(tk+1,x0))(x(t_{k},x_{0}),x(t_{k+1},x_{0})). Then, νk=(Id,ϕΔ​t)#​ρ​(tk)\nu_{k}=(\operatorname{Id},\phi_{\Delta t})_{\#}\rho(t_{k}), where ϕΔ​t\phi_{\Delta t} denotes the flow map of (1) over a step Δ​t{\Delta t}. Hence, the conditional law of x⁡(tk+1,x0)x(t_{k+1},x_{0}) given x⁡(tk,x0)x(t_{k},x_{0}) is the Dirac measure at ϕΔ​t​(x⁡(tk,x0))\phi_{\Delta t}(x(t_{k},x_{0})), and the coupling is deterministic.22 2 Under the simplifying assumption of noise-free observations. In FM, by contrast, the coupling is typically independent or chosen for computational convenience, and the associated velocity field transporting ρ⁡(tk)\rho(t_{k}) to ρ⁡(tk+1)\rho(t_{k+1}) does not necessarily coincide with the physical dynamics. In the present setting, the assumption of observing trajectories already yields a coupling between adjacent time steps, so that in VM each interpolant segment is anchored to an observed trajectory, and a single velocity field f^\hat{f} is shared across all intervals, effectively approximating the underlying ff. The choice of coupling, and of the resulting probability path, becomes instead essential when only the marginals {ρ⁡(tk)}k=0Nt\{\rho(t_{k})\}_{k=0}^{{N_{t}}} are observed, as in stochastic or population dynamics settings [Neklyudov et al., 2023, Lavenant et al., 2024, Berman et al., 2024, Blickhan et al., 2025], where trajectories need to be inferred.

4.2 Objective decomposition and implicit integration

Here we address the connection between VM and implicit Runge-Kutta (IRK) schemes, and discuss its implications. We first isolate the two contributions governing the VM objective, through a bias-variance decomposition of the loss (28), induced by its stochastic formulation with respect to the random offset τ\tau. To establish the subsequent results, we impose further regularity requirements on both the target and learnable velocity fields, requiring Lipschitz continuity in time, in addition to the Lipschitz continuity in space already assumed in Section 3.

Assumption 3.

Denoting by KK the closed δ\delta-neighborhood of the convex hull of the reachable set 𝒳\mathcal{X} defined in (2), both target and learnable velocity fields, ff and f^\hat{f}, belong to the function class

ℱ={g∈Wloc1,∞​(ℝn+1,ℝn):‖g‖W1,∞​([0,T]×K,ℝn)≤M},\mathcal{F}=\left\{g\in W^{1,\infty}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1};\mathbb{R}^{n}):\|g\|_{W^{1,\infty}([0,T]\times K;\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq M\right\}, (29)

for some δ>0\delta>0 and M>0M>0.

This assumption ensures that the stability constants introduced in Section 3, as well as interpolation error bounds, can be controlled uniformly. The following proposition establishes the bias-variance decomposition of the VM loss, which is proved in Appendix C.2.

The decomposition (30) holds with equality, with the two terms carrying distinct roles. The variance term accounts for the deviation of f^\hat{f} along the interpolant, and is the contribution of the stochastic offset τ\tau to the loss, unavailable through any deterministic collocation rule; its regularizing effect on the Jacobian of the learned velocity field is discussed in Section 4.4. The bias term reads as a continuous collocation condition averaged over the subinterval [tk,tk+1][t_{k},t_{k+1}], namely

|vk​(x0)−𝔼τ​[f^k​(τ,x0)]|=|1Δ​t​∫tktk+1(f⁡(t,x⁡(t,x0))−f^​(t,x~​(t,x0)))​𝑑t|,\big|v_{k}(x_{0})-\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[\hat{f}_{k}(\tau;x_{0})]\big|=\left|\frac{1}{{\Delta t}}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\left(f(t,x(t,x_{0}))-\hat{f}(t,\tilde{x}(t,x_{0}))\right)dt\right|, (31)

having used the identity vk​(x0)=Δ​t−1​∫tktk+1∂tx⁡(t,x0)​𝑑tv_{k}(x_{0})={\Delta t}^{-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\partial_{t}x(t,x_{0})dt, by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Enforcing the ODE residual at a single node tk+γ​Δ​tt_{k}+\gamma{\Delta t}, with γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1], on a polynomial of degree 1, is equivalent to a one-stage method with tableau a11=c1=γa_{11}=c_{1}=\gamma and b1=1b_{1}=1, implicit for γ>0\gamma>0, by the equivalence between collocation methods and IRK schemes [Hairer et al., 2008, Theorem 7.7]. Given such a correspondence, the VM bias term can be interpreted as a TF update, where the single-step update is performed via an IRK method, with the collocation point γ\gamma sampled uniformly within the subinterval. Proposition 4.3 establishes such an equivalence, where the VM bias term is identified with the residual of a continuous-stage Runge-Kutta (csRK) method, which generalizes IRK methods to a continuum of stages. The resulting csRK scheme associated with VM bias recovers the average vector field method [Quispel and McLaren, 2008, Hairer, 2010], of order 2, A-stable and, in the case of Hamiltonian systems, energy preserving [Celledoni et al., 2009].

The proof, along with details on csRK schemes, is provided in Appendix C.2. Denoting by FF the increment function associated with the csRK method, performing a TF update with an implicit scheme requires solving x^k+1=x⁡(tk,x0)+Δ​t​F​(tk,x⁡(tk,x0),x^k+1,Δ​t,f^)\hat{x}_{k+1}=x(t_{k},x_{0})+{\Delta t}F(t_{k},x(t_{k},x_{0}),\hat{x}_{k+1},{\Delta t};\hat{f}) for the predicted state x^k+1\hat{x}_{k+1}, so that the residual εk+1TF​(x0)\varepsilon_{k+1}^{\rm TF}(x_{0}) can be formed. Thus, although TF is simulation-free, training would still require differentiating through the nonlinear solver, at a computational cost that scales with the number of iterations required for convergence. The VM bias, instead, avoids the implicit solve by directly evaluating the residual at the observed pair (x⁡(tk,x0),x⁡(tk+1,x0))(x(t_{k},x_{0}),x(t_{k+1},x_{0})). In this sense, the VM objective carries the implicit method inside the optimization process, rather than in the forward pass, with the nonlinear system that a rollout or TF objective would require to solve at each step being replaced by a residual that the learned velocity field has to satisfy along the interpolant. Such a correspondence is made quantitative by the bounds (33), which relate the two residuals up to multiplicative factors, showing that minimizing the VM bias term is equivalent to minimizing the residual of a TF update coupled with an IRK method. In terms of stability properties, when considering the Dahlquist test equation x˙=λ​x\dot{x}=\lambda x, with λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}, as in Section 2, the stability function associated with the average vector field method reads as R⁡(z)=1+z/21−z/2R(z)=\frac{1+z/2}{1-z/2}, with z=λ​Δ​tz=\lambda{\Delta t}, so that |R⁡(z)|≤1|R(z)|\leq 1 for Re⁡(z)≤0\operatorname{Re}(z)\leq 0, yielding an A-stable method, namely a method whose stability region covers the entire left half of the complex plane. In particular, RR coincides with the stability function of the implicit midpoint method, which is a second-order A-stable method. This property, inherited by the VM bias term, agrees with the findings of Lu and Tsai [2026], where the implicit midpoint rule is shown to be a principled choice for learning conservative or dissipative dynamics, preserving structural properties of the underlying system.

4.3 Discretization bias, order of convergence and consistency

The VM objective is an empirical surrogate of the theoretical velocity objective (10), and is therefore biased. We identify two sources of bias, both stemming from the discrete nature of observations over time. First, the velocity target is estimated by a first-order finite difference vk​(x0)v_{k}(x_{0}), being the derivative of the piecewise linear interpolant. Second, the L2L^{2}-norm in time is approximated by uniformly sampling the offset τ\tau, and by evaluating the learned velocity field across the continuum of the interpolant, framing VM as a stochastic quadrature rule. The first source of bias is common to other empirical velocity-based objectives, as, for instance, in TF coupled with a first-order explicit Euler update (7). In this view, the distinguishing feature of VM lies in its stochastic collocation strategy, which, as shown below, yields an improved order of convergence in Δ​t{\Delta t} in the approximation of the theoretical velocity loss ℓf\ell_{f}, as compared to what TF attains.

The proof is provided in Appendix C.3, alongside a similar result for TF, which is shown to be of order O⁡(Δ​t)O({\Delta t}) rather than O⁡(Δ​t2)O({\Delta t}^{2}), thus highlighting the improved order of convergence of VM. The proof relies on the decomposition (30), whose terms are compared with the corresponding terms in the decomposition of the theoretical velocity loss ℓf\ell_{f}, and separately bounded. The bias terms differ through the velocity target, and through the argument at which the learned velocity field is evaluated, namely the interpolant in the case of ℓf,NtVM\ell_{f,{N_{t}}}^{\rm{VM}}. Chord estimates, provided in Lemma C.1, bound this difference by O⁡(Δ​t2)O({\Delta t}^{2}). The variance terms are separately O⁡(Δ​t2)O({\Delta t}^{2}), both integrands being Lipschitz in τ\tau, with constant controlled by MM. The estimate is a statement about the objective at fixed f^\hat{f}, and is uniform over ℱ\mathcal{F}, and it therefore transfers to the minimizers of the two objectives. In particular, combined with the previously established stability estimates, the following corollary closes the chain of estimates begun in Section 3, bounding the trajectory loss ℓx\ell_{x} in terms of the VM loss ℓf,NtVM\ell_{f,{N_{t}}}^{\rm{VM}}, and accounting for the discretization bias in Δ​t{\Delta t}.

The proof is provided in Appendix C.3. The right hand side of (36) is computable, and requires no simulation of the learned dynamics, as it only depends on the training loss ℓf,NtVM\ell_{f,{N_{t}}}^{\rm{VM}} plus an explicit discretization bias, with constants depending on the hypothesis class ℱ\mathcal{F} alone. Neither term requires solving (3), so that the bound is simulation-free, overcoming the need for backpropagation through an ODE solver, as instead required by the trajectory loss ℓx\ell_{x} on the left hand side. The smallness condition (35) is a technical requirement, as it yields confinement of the learned flow within KK, under the δ\delta-neighborhood of Assumption 3, without which the stability estimates of Lemma 3.3 would not hold. A similar argument has been employed in the proof of Theorem 3.8.

As a consequence of the previous result, we establish the consistency of the minimizer f^∗\hat{f}_{\ast} of the VM objective ℒf,N,NtVM\mathcal{L}_{f,N,{N_{t}}}^{\rm{VM}} with the true velocity field ff, in the L2L^{2} sense, as Δ​t→0{\Delta t}\to 0.

The proof is provided in Appendix C.3. The result is stated in terms of the empirical occupation measure μN\mu_{N}, for a finite set of observed trajectories, associated to sample of initial conditions of size NN from the prescribed distribution ρ0\rho_{0}, relying on the notation of Section 3.1.

4.4 Implicit regularization and Jacobian matching

The analysis carried out in the previous sections relies on a standing bound on the Lipschitz constant of the learned velocity field f^\hat{f}, which, for a continuously differentiable field on a convex domain, is equivalent to a bound on the norm of its Jacobian ∂xf^\partial_{x}\hat{f}. Such a bound enters the stability estimates of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, through the Gronwall constants depending on Lip⁡[f^]\operatorname{Lip}[\hat{f}], and is required by the approximation results of Section 4.3. Likewise, Assumption 3, on which the subsequent analysis of the VM objective relies, enforces a uniform bound of a similar nature. In practice, such a bound may be enforced through a penalty on the norm of ∂xf^\partial_{x}\hat{f}. However, the proof of Theorem 3.8, carried out in W1,∞W^{1,\infty}-norm, makes clear that controlling the norm of the learned Jacobian alone is not sufficient, as what should be controlled is its distance from the true Jacobian ∂xf\partial_{x}f. Indeed, arbitrary penalties on the Jacobian norm of the learned velocity field may steer the learning towards trivial solutions with arbitrarily small Jacobian norm, yielding sub-optimal approximation of the true velocity field ff; whereas, directly enforcing Jacobian matching, which has been shown to yield statistically accurate learning of chaotic dynamics [Park et al., 2024], is infeasible in the present setting, as ∂xf\partial_{x}f is not accessible, and its computation would require O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) complexity.

In this section, we show that, relying on the bias-variance decomposition (30), VM implicitly provides a form of Jacobian control, and that the role of the perturbation τ\tau along the interpolant decouples. Specifically, the bias term gives rise to a penalty on the mismatch between the Jacobians’ action on the true velocity, yielding a property which we refer to as implicit Jacobian matching. The variance term penalizes the action of the learned Jacobian on the true velocity, hence acting as a regularizer. As the following argument relies on a Taylor expansion of the bias and variance terms, we require further regularity, which is enforced by the following assumption.

Assumption 4.

Let KK be as in Assumption 3 and M>0M>0. Both target and learnable velocity fields, ff and f^\hat{f}, are autonomous and belong to the function class

ℱ={g∈Wloc2,∞​(ℝn,ℝn):‖g‖W2,∞​(K,ℝn)≤M}.\mathcal{F}=\left\{g\in W^{2,\infty}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{n};\mathbb{R}^{n}):\|g\|_{W^{2,\infty}(K;\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq M\right\}. (38)

The following result formalizes the above observations.

The proof is provided in Appendix C.4. The first claim holds in the regime where the learned velocity field is O⁡(Δ​t2)O({\Delta t}^{2})-close to the true one at the observed points. There, the remaining terms in the bias expansion are of higher order, and the leading order term reduces to (39), namely a directional Jacobian matching condition. As a consequence, in this regime, the VM objective implicitly enforces a penalty on the mismatch between the Jacobians’ action on the true velocity, which, while weaker than full Jacobian matching, emerges naturally from the stochastic collocation strategy employed by VM, as shown empirically in Section 5. The second claim holds without the closeness condition, and shows that the variance term induces a penalty on the action of the Jacobian of the learned velocity field on the true velocity, weighted by the variance Varτ⁡[τ]=Δ​t2/12\operatorname{Var}_{\tau}[\tau]={\Delta t}^{2}/12 of the perturbation τ∼𝒰⁡[0,Δ​t]\tau\sim\mathcal{U}[0,{\Delta t}]. By contrast with an arbitrary penalty on the Jacobian norm, it constrains only the variation of the learned velocity field along the flow, leaving the directions transverse to the flow unconstrained. This is a direct contribution of the random perturbation along the interpolant, as a deterministic collocation rule with a fixed offset τ\tau would yield a vanishing variance term, so that an equivalent control would have to be enforced explicitly.

To understand the effect of such a penalty on the learned flow, we may proceed formally. If the learned velocity field is sufficiently close to the true one, replacing the true trajectory and velocity with their learned counterparts in (40) yields

∂xf^​(x⁡(tk,x0))​f​(x⁡(tk,x0))≈∂xf^​(x^​(tk,x0))​f^​(x^​(tk,x0))=∂t2x^​(tk,x0),\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x(t_{k},x_{0}))f(x(t_{k},x_{0}))\approx\partial_{x}\hat{f}(\hat{x}(t_{k},x_{0}))\hat{f}(\hat{x}(t_{k},x_{0}))=\partial_{t}^{2}\hat{x}(t_{k},x_{0}),

so that the variance term acts as a penalty on the acceleration of the learned system. In this sense, its role is akin to that of cubic spline interpolation, where the natural interpolant minimizes the acceleration among sufficiently smooth interpolants. This analogy is only qualitative, since VM does not enforce interpolation of the learned trajectory at the observed points, its main aim being to reframe the learning problem as velocity regression rather than trajectory fitting. Nevertheless, it provides an intuitive interpretation of the regularization effect induced by the stochastic collocation strategy on the learned flow. Finally, both penalties are of order Δ​t2{\Delta t}^{2}, so that the implicit regularization does not degrade the order of convergence of the VM loss to the theoretical velocity loss established in Theorem 4.4.

5 Numerical results

Having characterized the velocity matching (VM) objective analytically, we now assess its behavior empirically. In Section 3, we showed that the trajectory error is controlled by a simulation-free quadratic objective over velocities; in Section 4, we showed that VM approximates such an objective to second order in the temporal step size of the observations, while implicitly matching the action of the Jacobians of the learned and true velocity fields along the flow. In this section, we investigate these properties numerically, by comparing VM with trajectory-based strategies reviewed in Section 2.2, on a range of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and spatially semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) benchmarks. In particular, Section 5.1 concerns a comparison in terms of accuracy attained by the different training strategies as a function of their training cost. Section 5.2 assesses the continuous-time approximation properties of the learned models, namely whether they can be simulated with a time step different from the one used during training, or with arbitrary Runge–Kutta schemes, without degrading the approximation error. Finally, Section 5.3 investigates properties specific to Hamiltonian and chaotic systems, namely the preservation of invariants and the reproduction of chaotic attractors.

Benchmark systems.

As ODEs, we consider the Euler equations of a free rigid body, namely a Lie–Poisson system whose trajectories lie on the unit sphere, and which conserves both its kinetic energy and a Casimir invariant; the Stuart–Landau oscillator, which is a normal form of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation whose trajectories are attracted by a stable limit cycle; an active particle in the Müller–Brown potential characterized by sustained oscillations within the potential wells; and the Lorenz system in its chaotic regime. As PDEs, we consider one-dimensional viscous Burgers, Fisher–KPP and Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equations, and the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) equation in its chaotic regime. Their spatial semi-discretization yields a high-dimensional ODE system, so that the learning problem falls within the setting of Section 2, with the learned velocity field acting on the discretized state. Further details are provided in Appendix D.

Experimental setup.

A common setup is adopted for all numerical experiments, in which models trained by minimizing the VM loss (28), according to Algorithm 1, are compared with models trained on the multiple-shooting rollout loss (6) in five configurations, spanning the single-step and multi-step settings of Section 2.2: teacher forcing (TF), namely L=1L=1; fixed shooting lengths L=5L=5 and L=10L=10; a randomized shooting length drawn uniformly in {1,…,20}\{1,\dots,20\} at each iteration; and a curriculum strategy, in which the shooting length grows linearly from L=1L=1 to L=50L=50 along training. Simulation of the learned dynamics in rollout training relies on explicit Euler updates, the typical scheme adopted for neural surrogates. For a given benchmark system, all training strategies share the same data, architecture, and optimization hyperparameters, so that the resulting models differ only in the objective being minimized. The accuracy of the learned dynamics is measured by the relative L2L^{2} error between reference and learned trajectories over the time interval [0,T][0,T], with TT denoting either the validation or test horizon,

ℰtraj\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{traj}} :=𝔼x0∼ρ0​‖x⁡(⋅,x0)−x^​(⋅,x0)‖L2​([0,T],ℝn)‖x⁡(⋅,x0)‖L2​([0,T],ℝn),\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim\rho_{0}}\frac{\|x(\cdot,x_{0})-\hat{x}(\cdot,x_{0})\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}}{\|x(\cdot,x_{0})\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}}, (Trajectory error) (41)

where x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}) and x^​(t,x0)\hat{x}(t,x_{0}) denote the solutions of the target and learned systems, respectively. In particular, training and validation share the same temporal horizon, Tvalid=TtrainT_{\mathrm{valid}}=T_{\mathrm{train}}, whereas testing is performed over a horizon twice as long, Ttest=2​TtrainT_{\mathrm{test}}=2T_{\mathrm{train}}, so that the test set assesses both generalization to unseen initial conditions and time extrapolation. For the ODE benchmarks, the true velocity field ff and its Jacobian ∂xf\partial_{x}f are available, so that the accuracy of the learned field itself can also be measured, through the following relative errors

ℰvel\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{vel}} :=𝔼x0∼ρ0​‖f⁡(x⁡(⋅,x0))−f^​(x⁡(⋅,x0))‖L2​([0,T],ℝn)‖f⁡(x⁡(⋅,x0))‖L2​([0,T],ℝn),\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim\rho_{0}}\frac{\|f(x(\cdot,x_{0}))-\hat{f}(x(\cdot,x_{0}))\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}}{\|f(x(\cdot,x_{0}))\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}}, (Velocity error) (42)
ℰJac\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{Jac}} :=𝔼x0∼ρ0​‖∂xf⁡(x⁡(⋅,x0))−∂xf^​(x⁡(⋅,x0))‖L2​([0,T],ℝn×n)‖∂xf⁡(x⁡(⋅,x0))‖L2​([0,T],ℝn×n),\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim\rho_{0}}\frac{\|\partial_{x}f(x(\cdot,x_{0}))-\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x(\cdot,x_{0}))\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n\times n})}}{\|\partial_{x}f(x(\cdot,x_{0}))\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n\times n})}}, (Jacobian error) (43)

with ℝn×n\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} equipped with the Frobenius norm. Note that both quantities are evaluated along the reference trajectories x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}), rather than the learned ones, as they measure the discrepancy between the velocity fields on the support of the data, independently of the error accumulated by integrating the learned dynamics. Together, the velocity and Jacobian errors provide an L2L^{2} proxy, along the reference trajectories, for the W1,∞W^{1,\infty} error of f^\hat{f} on which our approximation results rely. In practice, we report the empirical counterparts of (41)–(43), in which the expectation over initial conditions and the time integrals are replaced by sample averages. Each training objective was run with three independent seeds, and, for each run, the model attaining the lowest validation trajectory error (41) was retained for testing. Further details are given in Appendix D.

5.1 Accuracy, fast convergence and implicit regularization

We first compare the proposed VM objective against TF and rollout training strategies in terms of accuracy and of the computational cost required to attain it, under a common iteration budget, on both ODE and PDE benchmarks. For the ODE benchmarks, we then assess how the learned velocity fields and their Jacobians compare with the true ones.

Accuracy and training efficiency.

Figure 5 reports, for the Euler, Stuart–Landau and active Müller–Brown systems, the evolution of the three validation errors (41-43) against elapsed training time, alongside the test trajectory error attained by each seed, plotted against the total training time of the corresponding run. The former shows how fast each objective reduces the validation errors during training, whereas the latter relates the final test accuracy to the overall computational cost under the common iteration budget. The corresponding validation and test errors are collected in Table 3 in Appendix D. Two observations hold across all three test cases. First, VM and TF have a comparable cost per iteration, since both evaluate f^\hat{f} once per sample, as discussed in Section 4.1, while, by contrast, the cost of the rollout-based strategies grows with the shooting length LL, as their gradients are obtained by backpropagating through LL explicit Euler steps. Second, all trajectory-based strategies saturate at a common error level, in all three metrics and irrespective of LL, whereas the validation errors of VM keep decreasing well below such a level, within a training time comparable with that of TF. On the test set, VM reduces the trajectory error by up to an order of magnitude relative to rollout strategies, consistently across test cases and seeds, whereas the latter yield test errors of 10−110^{-1} or larger. A comparable reduction is observed in the velocity and Jacobian errors. These observations are consistent with the analysis carried out in the previous sections. Although VM never simulates the learned dynamics during training, it attains the lowest trajectory error, as expected from Corollary 4.5, by which the trajectory loss is controlled by the VM loss up to a discretization bias of order Δ​t2{\Delta t}^{2}. By contrast, the TF objective approximates the theoretical velocity objective only to first order in Δ​t{\Delta t} (Theorem C.2), with its minimizers inheriting the corresponding bias. Longer shooting horizons do not remove this bias, since the same explicit Euler update is adopted, but rather reshape the loss landscape, as discussed in Section 2.3.

Analogously, Figure 6 reports, for the Burgers, Fisher–KPP, and KdV equations, the evolution of the validation trajectory error against elapsed training time, alongside the test trajectory error attained by each seed against the total training time of the corresponding run. In this case, the spatial discretization of the PDE solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t)33 3 In the PDE setting, we denote by uu the solution and by xx the spatial coordinate, the latter not to be confused with the state of (1), which here corresponds to the discretized solution uhu_{h}, with hh the spatial discretization step. yields a 10241024-dimensional time-dependent state uh​(t)u_{h}(t), whose evolution is governed by a system of the form (1), in which the vector field ff corresponds to the spatially discretized differential operator on the right-hand side of the PDE, approximated by the learned one f^\hat{f}. Validation and test trajectory errors for each equation and training strategy, averaged across seeds, are collected in Table 4 of Appendix D, while Figures 11–13 report the pointwise absolute errors on four test trajectories per equation. Unlike in the ODE test cases, the dependence of the validation and test errors on the shooting length LL is strongly problem-dependent. For the Fisher–KPP equation, both errors improve slightly as LL increases, whereas for the Burgers and KdV equations rollout training exhibits instabilities that become more pronounced for larger LL. By contrast, VM – using the same architecture and optimization hyperparameters – yields stable optimization procedure on all three test cases with the validation trajectory error steadily decreasing throughout training without the instabilities observed for rollout objectives. The retained models attain the lowest test errors across equations and seeds. This is consistent with the analysis of Section 2.3, which shows that the smoothness of trajectory-based objectives deteriorates as the rollout length LL increases, with gradients that vanish or explode exponentially in LL, thus hindering the convergence of gradient-based optimization.

Velocity approximation.

The velocity error (42) measures the accuracy of the learned field along the reference trajectories in an averaged L2L^{2} sense. Figure 7 complements it by showing the pointwise error over the state space of the Stuart–Landau and active Müller–Brown systems. The error of VM is lowest over the region spanned by the training trajectories, namely around the limit cycle and along the transients spiraling towards it for the former, and within the potential wells for the latter, and grows away from this region. This agrees with the variational characterization of Proposition 3.2, by which the minimizer of the velocity objective is determined only on the support of the occupation measure (12), and is left unconstrained elsewhere. Corollary 4.6 transfers this characterization to the empirical VM objective, whose minimizer is O⁡(Δ​t2)O({\Delta t}^{2})-consistent with ff on the same support. Although TF also admits a velocity regression reading, its validation velocity error plateaus at the same level as that of rollout training, as shown in Figure 5, suggesting that its O⁡(Δ​t)O({\Delta t}) bias, compounded by the spectral constraints induced by the explicit Euler step, limits the attainable accuracy. The gap between the pointwise errors of VM and rollout training in Figure 7 reflects a structural difference between the two objectives, as rollout training does not recover the true velocity field ff, but rather the field that, when numerically simulated with the scheme and time step used during training, best reproduces the observed trajectories. This aspect will be further addressed in Section 5.2, since continuous-time approximation hinges on the capability of recovering ff itself.

Implicit Jacobian matching.

As shown in Proposition 4.7, the bias term of the VM loss aligns the action of the learned Jacobian with that of the true Jacobian along the flow, without having access to the latter, while its variance term penalizes the variation of the learned field along the flow. Neither mechanism is available to TF, which evaluates f^\hat{f} only at the observed states, or to rollout training, which relies on the same explicit Euler update. The Jacobian errors (43) in Figure 5 are consistent with this picture. Indeed, although no information about the Jacobians is provided, the Jacobian error of VM decreases steadily throughout training, and, as reported in Table 3, its test value is lower than that of the trajectory-based strategies by a factor of 3–9 across the three test cases. We stress that Jacobian accuracy matters beyond velocity accuracy, since the Jacobian of the vector field governs the local behavior of the dynamics, determining the stability of equilibria, as well as the rates at which nearby trajectories contract or separate. An accurate Jacobian thus preserves the qualitative structure of the target dynamics, and keeps the stability constants entering Lemma 3.3 close to those of the true system.

5.2 Continuous-time approximation

Formulating a model in continuous time, as an ODE, does not by itself guarantee that, once trained on observations at a fixed step, it can be simulated with other step sizes and numerical schemes without loss of accuracy. Theorem 3.9 guarantees this property for a learned velocity field that is close to ff in W1,∞W^{1,\infty}, through the decomposition (24) of the error into the continuous-time error of the learned flow and the discretization error of the scheme. We assess the continuous-time approximation capability of the models learned by VM, TF, and the selected rollout strategies by studying the test trajectory error as a function of the step size Δ​t{\Delta t} used at inference. Figure 8 reports this error against Δ​t{\Delta t} for the Euler, Stuart–Landau, and active Müller–Brown systems, with Δ​t{\Delta t} ranging from 10−410^{-4} to well beyond the training step size, and with each column corresponding to an explicit Runge–Kutta scheme of order p∈{1,2,4}p\in\{1,2,4\}. In all cases, the reference trajectories are computed with step size 10−410^{-4} and interpolated onto the coarser grids. Beyond assessing whether the learned model can be simulated on temporal grids other than the training one without retraining, a critical computational aspect for neural surrogates, this experiment also serves as a proxy for the closeness of f^\hat{f} to ff. By (24), the error of a model close to ff should follow that of ff itself for large Δ​t{\Delta t}, where the discretization error dominates, and saturate at the continuous-time error of the learned flow as Δ​t→0{\Delta t}\to 0. We therefore restrict this experiment to the ODE benchmarks, where ff is available in closed form, so that the error attained by integrating ff with the same schemes and step sizes (dashed green lines) is used as a reference. Note that, since Theorem 3.9 is an approximation result, as it requires f^\hat{f} to be close to ff on a region containing the trajectories of interest, continuous-time approximation would naturally be assessed on the training trajectories. Here, we instead evaluate the error on an additional test set, since such a property is of practical interest only if it holds for unseen initial conditions, thus yielding a more challenging setting that combines approximation and generalization errors.

The error associated with VM exactly follows the decomposition (24). For large step sizes, it coincides with the error obtained by integrating the true velocity field with the same scheme, and decreases at rate Δ​tp{\Delta t}^{p}, since the discretization error dominates. Following such a decomposition, this formally indicates that a field f^\hat{f} sufficiently close to ff in W1,∞W^{1,\infty} has been learned, even though everything here is measured in L2L^{2} norms. As the step size decreases, it saturates at a plateau that does not depend on the scheme, but rather on the continuous-time approximation error ‖x−x^‖L∞\|x-\hat{x}\|_{L^{\infty}} of the learned flow, and is in all cases smaller than or equal to the error attained at the training discretization, so that the accuracy is not affected, thus yielding a model that can handle finer discretizations. Consistently, the plateau is reached at larger step sizes as the order pp increases, since the discretization error falls below the continuous-time error sooner for higher-order schemes.

The errors associated with rollout strategies behave differently. When integrated with explicit Euler (RK1), the scheme used for training, their error attains a sharp minimum at the training step size, and increases as the step size is refined, until it saturates at a plateau well above both their minimum and the VM plateau, which instead retains the training accuracy. Moreover, higher-order schemes do not improve their accuracy at any step size. Thus, the velocity field learned via rollouts is accurate only when combined with the scheme and step size used for training. So, the picture outlined in the previous section repeats, since, rather than approximating ff, the model learns an Euler update that compensates for the discretization error of the scheme, thus overfitting the training discretization. This is the empirical counterpart of the decomposition (20), which shows that TF minimizes the residual of the numerical scheme rather than the mismatch between velocity fields, and is in agreement with the observations of Krishnapriyan et al. [2023]. By contrast, the VM objective approximates the theoretical velocity objective ℒf\mathcal{L}_{f} to second order in Δ​t{\Delta t} without reference to any integrator (Theorem 4.4), yielding a learned velocity field that can be simulated with arbitrary schemes and step sizes at inference.

5.3 Learning Hamiltonian and chaotic dynamics

Finally, we consider systems characterized by relevant qualitative features, possibly emerging over long times, namely the preservation of invariants and the structure of chaotic attractors. Since none of the tested objectives enforces these features explicitly, they provide an indirect test of the accuracy of the learned velocity field and its Jacobian.

Euler.

The Euler equations of a free rigid body conserve the kinetic energy, namely the Hamiltonian HH, and the Casimir invariant C⁡(x)=|x|2C(x)=|x|^{2}, so that trajectories lie on the unit sphere. As shown in Figure 9, the trajectories learned by VM conserve both invariants up to small fluctuations, over a test horizon twice as long as the training one. By contrast, those learned by TF and by the rollout-based strategies drift monotonically, and lose approximately 15%15\% of HH and 10%10\% of CC by the end of the horizon, which reveals a systematic dissipation in the learned dynamics. Such dissipation is consistent with Proposition 2.2, by which training through explicit Euler updates constrains the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to lie within the stability region of the scheme, and hence towards contractive dynamics. Note that, for conservative dynamics such as the rigid body, the linearization about a stationary rotation around the major or minor axis [Marsden and Ratiu, 1999, Theorem 15.9.1] has purely imaginary eigenvalues [Marsden and Ratiu, 1999, Eq. (15.9.12)] when restricted to the tangent space at the equilibrium of the unit sphere in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, which therefore lie outside the stability region of explicit Euler for every step size. By contrast, the VM objective does not push the spectrum of the learned Jacobian off the imaginary axis, since its bias term is the residual of the average vector field method (Proposition 4.3), whose stability function satisfies |R⁡(z)|=1|R(z)|=1 on the imaginary axis. As a result, the learned system preserves the structural properties of the reference dynamics.

Lorenz.

In the chaotic regime, where pointwise trajectory errors become uninformative beyond a few Lyapunov times, the relevant question is whether the learned dynamics reproduces the attractor. We consider the case of the Lorenz system [Lorenz, 1963], with training trajectories starting from initial conditions sampled from a concentrated distribution ρ0≈δx0\rho_{0}\approx\delta_{x_{0}}. We vary the training step size Δ​t{\Delta t} from 10−310^{-3} to 10−110^{-1}, and report the orbits of the learned systems for Δ​t=2⋅10−2{\Delta t}=2\cdot 10^{-2} in Figure 9, alongside the spectrum of the Jacobian of the learned dynamics at the critical point C−C_{-}, for the considered range of training step sizes Δ​t{\Delta t}. The latter explains the collapse of TF trajectories onto C−C_{-} in Figure 9, and analogously for the rollout strategies. For the true dynamics, the two critical points C±C_{\pm}, other than the origin, are unstable [Sparrow, 1982]. Their complex-conjugate eigenvalues have a small, but positive, real part, which makes trajectories escape from their neighborhood and switch between the two regions of the attractor. As the training step size increases, TF and the rollout-based strategies learn complex eigenvalues with an increasingly negative real part, so that C−C_{-} becomes a stable equilibrium, inducing the collapse of trajectories onto it. This stabilization, a consequence of the spectral constraint of Proposition 2.2, prevents the chaotic dynamics and its attractor from being learned. By contrast, VM recovers the real part of these eigenvalues accurately over most of the range of step sizes, in line with the implicit Jacobian matching mechanism of Proposition 4.7. We stress that, although formal, the connection between VM and Jacobian matching strategies, established through the implicit regularization result of Proposition 4.7, becomes relevant when learning statistically accurate chaotic dynamics. Indeed, Park et al. [2024] showed, through an ergodic-theoretic analysis based on shadowing, that small errors in the vector field alone do not guarantee the recovery of the invariant measure, whereas closeness of both the learned dynamics and its Jacobian does, proposing, consistently, to augment the regression loss with a Jacobian matching term. This approach has recently been extended by Kang et al. [2026], who match Jacobians at randomly perturbed states to implicitly enforce second-order consistency. Both strategies, however, require access to the true Jacobian at the training states, and involve forming Jacobian matrices, at a cost of O⁡(n)O(n) derivative evaluations and O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory per training state. By contrast, VM only matches the action of the Jacobian along the flow, which stochastic collocation extracts from trajectory data alone at the cost of a single evaluation of f^\hat{f} per collocation point, without forming any Jacobian.

Kuramoto–Sivashinsky.

We conclude with the KS equation on a periodic domain of length 6464, discretized on 256256 grid points, whose dynamics exhibits spatiotemporal chaos. Although the comparison between VM and TF is only qualitative, this test case extends the previous discussion to a high-dimensional setting. While the fourth-order term makes the semi-discretized system stiff [Kassam and Trefethen, 2005], the associated modes may decay on time scales much shorter than the sampling step Δ​t{\Delta t}, so that neither objective can identify them from the data. The two objectives differ instead in their treatment of the advective term, which transports the solution without dissipating it, and whose linearization thus has eigenvalues close to the imaginary axis [LeVeque, 2007]. As for the rigid body and the Lorenz system, TF compensates for the explicit Euler update by damping these modes, which acts as an additional diffusion on the learned dynamics. The training trajectories cover the time interval [0,200][0,200], while the test trajectories extend to T=800T=800. Figure 10 provides a qualitative comparison of the space-time evolution of the learned dynamics and of their statistics on the attractor, through the joint probability density of the first two spatial derivatives (∂xu,∂x2u)(\partial_{x}u,\partial_{x}^{2}u) [Linot and Graham, 2020]. Although individual trajectories decorrelate from the reference after a few Lyapunov times, as expected for chaotic dynamics, the dynamics learned by VM generates spatiotemporal chaos qualitatively similar to the true one, both within and well beyond the training horizon, and its joint density closely matches the reference. By contrast, the dynamics learned by TF evolves towards a more regular regime, dominated by low-wavenumber patterns, and its joint density concentrates around the origin, consistently with the spectral constraints induced by the explicit Euler bias, which damps the high-wavenumber content of the solution.

6 Conclusions

This work introduces Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free framework for learning continuous-time dynamical systems formulated as ordinary differential equations (ODEs), a task commonly formulated as the minimization of a trajectory-based objective. Beyond the computational cost associated with simulation-based training, we show that trajectory-based objectives suffer from structural degeneracies, which hinder gradient-based optimization and bias the learned dynamics, thus motivating the transition towards simulation-free velocity-based learning. To this end, we develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, in which the velocity field of the underlying ODE is characterized as the minimizer of a quadratic functional, and relate this objective to its trajectory-based counterpart through the introduction of suitable LpL^{p}-LqL^{q} stability estimates, which can be read as a Lax equivalence result in a learning setting. These estimates justify simulation-free training based on velocity supervision and enable us to establish a universal approximation result for the flow of the true dynamics by neural ODEs, whose velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. This result in turn allows us to characterize the continuous-time approximation property of the learned dynamics. Relying on this theoretical framework, we characterize the properties of the VM objective. In particular, through a bias-variance decomposition, we relate the VM loss to implicit integration and show that VM provides a higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk. Combined with the stability estimates, this result yields a simulation-free bound on the trajectory loss, alongside the consistency of the VM minimizer as the step size vanishes. Moreover, the same decomposition reveals an implicit regularization of the Jacobian of the learned field along the observed trajectories, connecting VM to Jacobian matching approaches, without requiring access to the true Jacobian. Numerical results on ODEs and semi-discretized time-dependent PDEs, featuring limit cycles as well as conservative and chaotic dynamics, support these findings, showing that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based strategies at a lower training cost.

Several questions remain open. The effect of the stochastic collocation of VM on specific classes of nonlinear dynamics, possibly with noisy observations, remains largely unexplored, and the analysis of Section 4 is only a first step in this direction. It would be valuable to clarify for which classes of systems, whether oscillatory, conservative, dissipative, or multiscale, stochastic collocation is most beneficial, as this could guide the design of collocation distributions that are adapted to specific classes of systems. Moreover, the constants appearing in the stability estimates of Section 3.2, on which the subsequent results rely, grow exponentially with the time horizon and the Lipschitz constant, as is common for Grönwall-type estimates, and may thus become uninformative. Specializing these estimates to specific classes of dynamics, by exploiting their structure, could yield sharper bounds and more informative guarantees for learning. Finally, although we have extended the stability estimates to a Wasserstein estimate, adopting an ergodic perspective could connect the implicit Jacobian regularization of VM to statistical guarantees on the invariant measures of chaotic dynamics.

Appendix A Additional results and proofs of Section 2

In this section we shall extend the discussion on the challenges of trajectory-based learning, presented in Section 2.3, by providing detailed arguments for the issues related to the optimization of the trajectory-based learning objective, in both continuous- and discrete-time settings.

A.1 Additional results of Section 2.3.1

To address the analysis of the trajectory-based learning objective a simplified setting is considered in which the target system is linear, and the learning problem is cast as a parameter identification one. This allows to derive closed-form expressions and to characterize the criticalities of the trajectory-based learning objective, alongside their dependence on the regime of the target and learned dynamics, as well as on the temporal horizon. Our main interest is in the limiting behavior of the loss landscape, and its higher-order derivatives, in the tails of the parameter space, as well as in the infinite-horizon limit, being the main sources of degeneracy in the loss landscape. Asymptotic expressions are derived, aiming at characterizing the rates at which such degeneracies occur, and the regimes in which they are more pronounced. Hence, we proceed by deriving explicit expressions for the energy-normalized trajectory objective, its gradient and Hessian, by considering the problem of learning a 1-dimensional linear system, with dynamics given by x˙=λ​x\dot{x}=\lambda x, for some λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. We cast such a problem into a parameter identification one, by considering a parametric family of linear systems, given by x^˙=λ^​x^\dot{\hat{x}}=\hat{\lambda}\hat{x}, with λ^∈ℝ\hat{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}. We assume the initial condition x⁡(0)=x^​(0)=x0x(0)=\hat{x}(0)=x_{0} to be fixed, and λ,λ^≠0\lambda,\hat{\lambda}\neq 0. The trajectory-based learning objective, for a single fixed initial condition x0x_{0}, normalized by the average trajectory energy, is defined as

ℓ¯x​(λ^,x0):=‖x⁡(⋅,x0)−x^​(⋅,x0)‖L2​([0,T],ℝ)2‖x⁡(⋅,x0)‖L2​([0,T],ℝ)2,\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda};x_{0}):=\frac{\|x(\cdot,x_{0})-\hat{x}(\cdot,x_{0})\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R})}^{2}}{\|x(\cdot,x_{0})\|_{L^{2}([0,T];\mathbb{R})}^{2}}, (44)

which, considering the explicit solution of the linear systems, can be expressed as

ℓ¯x​(λ^)=∫0T(eλ​t−eλ^​t)2​𝑑t∫0Te2​λ​t​𝑑t,\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda})=\frac{\int_{0}^{T}(e^{\lambda t}-e^{\hat{\lambda}t})^{2}dt}{\int_{0}^{T}e^{2\lambda t}dt},

thus depending only on the parameters λ,λ^\lambda,\hat{\lambda} and the time horizon TT. The normalization is introduced to ignore the scaling effects of the solution norm, initial condition and time horizon on the loss landscape, which would otherwise dominate in certain regimes. To perform explicit computations, we define the auxiliary moment function Mk​(ξ)=∫0Ttk​eξ​t​𝑑tM_{k}(\xi)=\int_{0}^{T}t^{k}e^{\xi t}dt, for ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, allowing to express the above objective, alongside its derivatives, in closed-form. In particular, kk-th order moments can be computed by means of integration by parts, yielding the following recursive formula

Mk​(ξ)=Tk​eξ​Tξ−kξ​Mk−1​(ξ),k∈ℕ≥1,ξ∈ℝ,ξ≠0,M_{k}(\xi)=\frac{T^{k}e^{\xi T}}{\xi}-\frac{k}{\xi}M_{k-1}(\xi),\quad k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},\quad\xi\in\mathbb{R},\ \xi\neq 0,

from which closed-form expressions for orders k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3 can be derived, resulting in

M0​(ξ)=eξ​T−1ξ,M1​(ξ)=(ξ​T−1)​eξ​T+1ξ2,M_{0}(\xi)=\frac{e^{\xi T}-1}{\xi},\qquad M_{1}(\xi)=\frac{(\xi T-1)e^{\xi T}+1}{\xi^{2}},
M2​(ξ)=(ξ2​T2−2​ξ​T+2)​eξ​T−2ξ3,M3​(ξ)=(ξ3​T3−3​ξ2​T2+6​ξ​T−6)​eξ​T+6ξ4.M_{2}(\xi)=\frac{(\xi^{2}T^{2}-2\xi T+2)e^{\xi T}-2}{\xi^{3}},\qquad M_{3}(\xi)=\frac{(\xi^{3}T^{3}-3\xi^{2}T^{2}+6\xi T-6)e^{\xi T}+6}{\xi^{4}}.

We recall the following identities for higher-order derivatives of the moment function, verifiable by direct differentiation,

∂ξkM0​(ξ)=Mk(ξ),k∈ℕ,∂ξM0​(h⁡(ξ))=h′​(ξ)​M1​(h⁡(ξ)),∂ξ2M0​(h⁡(ξ))=h′′​(ξ)​M1​(h⁡(ξ))+(h′​(ξ))2​M2​(h⁡(ξ)),∂ξ3M0​(h⁡(ξ))=h′′′​(ξ)​M1​(h⁡(ξ))+3​h′​(ξ)​h′′​(ξ)​M2​(h⁡(ξ))+(h′​(ξ))3​M3​(h⁡(ξ)),\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{\xi}^{k}M_{0}(\xi)&=M_{k}(\xi),\quad k\in\mathbb{N},\\ \partial_{\xi}M_{0}(h(\xi))&=h^{\prime}(\xi)M_{1}(h(\xi)),\\ \partial_{\xi}^{2}M_{0}(h(\xi))&=h^{\prime\prime}(\xi)M_{1}(h(\xi))+(h^{\prime}(\xi))^{2}M_{2}(h(\xi)),\\ \partial_{\xi}^{3}M_{0}(h(\xi))&=h^{\prime\prime\prime}(\xi)M_{1}(h(\xi))+3h^{\prime}(\xi)h^{\prime\prime}(\xi)M_{2}(h(\xi))+(h^{\prime}(\xi))^{3}M_{3}(h(\xi)),\end{split} (45)

with hh a sufficiently regular function of ξ\xi. Additionally, we recall the asymptotic behavior of the moment function, which is useful for characterizing the tail behavior of the loss landscape. For fixed T>0T>0 and ξ→±∞\xi\to\pm\infty,

limξ→−∞ξ​M0​(ξ)=−1,limξ→−∞ξ2​M1​(ξ)=1,Mk​(ξ)∼Tk​eξ​Tξ,ξ→+∞,\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}\xi M_{0}(\xi)=-1,\qquad\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}\xi^{2}M_{1}(\xi)=1,\qquad M_{k}(\xi)\sim\frac{T^{k}e^{\xi T}}{\xi},\quad\xi\to+\infty, (46)

while, in the infinite-horizon limit T→+∞T\to+\infty, for fixed ξ≠0\xi\neq 0, we have

Mk​(ξ)→k!|ξ|k+1,ξ<0,Mk​(ξ)∼Tk​eξ​Tξ,ξ>0.M_{k}(\xi)\to\frac{k!}{|\xi|^{k+1}},\quad\xi<0,\qquad M_{k}(\xi)\sim\frac{T^{k}e^{\xi T}}{\xi},\quad\xi>0. (47)

The behavior of the moment is what drives the asymmetric behavior and regime dependence of the loss landscape studied in the following, being dominated by the exponential growth of the moment for positive rates, and instead by saturation for negative rates.

Loss landscape analysis.

We proceed to derive closed-form expressions for the loss, gradient and Hessian of the energy-normalized trajectory objective (44). Relying on the explicit solution of the linear systems, with x⁡(t,x0)=eλ​t​x0x(t,x_{0})=e^{\lambda t}x_{0} and x^​(t,x0)=eλ^​t​x0\hat{x}(t,x_{0})=e^{\hat{\lambda}t}x_{0}, and the definition of the zero-th order moment, the loss can be expressed as

ℓ¯x​(λ^)\displaystyle\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda}) =1+M0​(2​λ^)M0​(2​λ)−2​M0​(λ^+λ)M0​(2​λ),\displaystyle=1+\frac{M_{0}(2\hat{\lambda})}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}-2\frac{M_{0}(\hat{\lambda}+\lambda)}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}, (48)
=1+λλ^​e2​λ^​T−1e2​λ​T−1−4​λλ+λ^​e(λ+λ^)​T−1e2​λ​T−1.\displaystyle=1+\frac{\lambda}{\hat{\lambda}}\frac{e^{2\hat{\lambda}T}-1}{e^{2\lambda T}-1}-\frac{4\lambda}{\lambda+\hat{\lambda}}\frac{e^{(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})T}-1}{e^{2\lambda T}-1}.

Differentiating the above with respect to λ^\hat{\lambda}, and using the moment identities (45), the closed-form expression for the gradient results in

∂λ^ℓ¯x​(λ^)\displaystyle\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda}) =2M0​(2​λ)​(M1​(2​λ^)−M1​(λ+λ^)),\displaystyle=\frac{2}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}\left(M_{1}(2\hat{\lambda})-M_{1}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})\right), (49)
=λλ^2​(2​λ^​T−1)​e2​λ^​T+1e2​λ​T−1−4​λ(λ+λ^)2​((λ+λ^)​T−1)​e(λ+λ^)​T+1e2​λ​T−1.\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{\hat{\lambda}^{2}}\frac{(2\hat{\lambda}T-1)e^{2\hat{\lambda}T}+1}{e^{2\lambda T}-1}-\frac{4\lambda}{(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})^{2}}\frac{((\lambda+\hat{\lambda})T-1)e^{(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})T}+1}{e^{2\lambda T}-1}.

Finally, applying again the moment identities (45) with h⁡(λ^)=2​λ^h(\hat{\lambda})=2\hat{\lambda} and h⁡(λ^)=λ+λ^h(\hat{\lambda})=\lambda+\hat{\lambda}, the Hessian of (44) with respect to λ^\hat{\lambda} is given by

∂λ^2ℓ¯x​(λ^)\displaystyle\partial^{2}_{\hat{\lambda}}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda}) =2M0​(2​λ)​(2​M2​(2​λ^)−M2​(λ+λ^)),\displaystyle=\frac{2}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}\left(2M_{2}(2\hat{\lambda})-M_{2}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})\right), (50)
=λλ^3​(4​λ^2​T2−4​λ^​T+2)​e2​λ^​T−2e2​λ​T−1−4​λ(λ+λ^)3​((λ+λ^)2​T2−2​(λ+λ^)​T+2)​e(λ+λ^)​T−2e2​λ​T−1.\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{\hat{\lambda}^{3}}\frac{(4\hat{\lambda}^{2}T^{2}-4\hat{\lambda}T+2)e^{2\hat{\lambda}T}-2}{e^{2\lambda T}-1}-\frac{4\lambda}{(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})^{3}}\frac{((\lambda+\hat{\lambda})^{2}T^{2}-2(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})T+2)e^{(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})T}-2}{e^{2\lambda T}-1}.

Given the closed-form expressions above, we characterize the landscape of ℓ¯x​(λ^)\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda}) through two results reading against the requirements of gradient-based optimization, namely degeneracy of the gradient and of the Hessian. In particular, we show that the loss landscape exhibits a regime-dependent behavior, with the presence of vanishing or exploding gradients, alongside ill-conditioning, and how the issues are made worse, at fast rates, in the infinite-horizon limit T→+∞T\to+\infty. Regarding the loss, it is immediate to verify that, for every fixed T>0T>0, the minimizer is attained at λ^=λ\hat{\lambda}=\lambda, with ℓ¯x​(λ)=0\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)=0. By the asymptotic behavior of the moment function (46), we have that the loss flattens out for λ^→−∞\hat{\lambda}\to-\infty, with ℓ¯x​(λ^)→1\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda})\to 1, while it inherits exponential growth for λ^→+∞\hat{\lambda}\to+\infty, with ℓ¯x​(λ^)∼M0​(2​λ^)/M0​(2​λ)\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda})\sim M_{0}(2\hat{\lambda})/M_{0}(2\lambda). Given that the loss is smooth, the presence of the horizontal asymptote, having a positive value, alongside with the presence of the minimizer at which the loss vanishes, implies a non-convex landscape. Considering the infinite-horizon limit T→+∞T\to+\infty, the loss landscape exhibits a transition between the two regimes, with the following limiting behavior

limT→+∞ℓ¯x​(λ^)={(λ−λ^)2λ^​(λ+λ^),λ<0,λ^<0,+∞,λ​<0,λ^>​0,limT→+∞ℓ¯x​(λ^)={1,λ>0,λ^<λ,0,λ>0,λ^=λ,+∞,λ>0,λ^>λ.\lim_{T\to+\infty}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda})=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(\lambda-\hat{\lambda})^{2}}{\hat{\lambda}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})},&\lambda<0,\ \hat{\lambda}<0,\\[10.0pt] +\infty,&\lambda<0,\ \hat{\lambda}>0,\end{cases}\qquad\lim_{T\to+\infty}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda})=\begin{cases}1,&\lambda>0,\ \hat{\lambda}<\lambda,\\ 0,&\lambda>0,\ \hat{\lambda}=\lambda,\\ +\infty,&\lambda>0,\ \hat{\lambda}>\lambda.\end{cases} (51)

Hence, the loss landscape converges to a smooth, non-convex profile in the dissipative regime λ<0\lambda<0, while it converges to a discontinuous function in the unstable regime λ>0\lambda>0, with a blow-up at λ^>λ\hat{\lambda}>\lambda happening in both cases. This is consistent with the intuition that learning in the unstable regime is a challenging task, and that increasing the time horizon may not be beneficial, with the collapse to a discontinuous landscape happening exponentially fast in TT.

It is legitimate to expect that, the flattening of the loss landscape in the dissipative regime, and the blow-up in the unstable one, induce vanishing and exploding gradients, respectively. In particular, the exponential nature of moments, and their asymptotic behavior, suggests that the rates at which such degeneracies occur are exponential in TT. We proceed to characterize the gradient of the loss landscape, being the main quantity of interest for gradient-based optimization. The following proposition characterizes the asymptotic behavior of the gradient, both in the tails (λ^→±∞)(\hat{\lambda}\to\pm\infty) and in the infinite-horizon limit (T→+∞)(T\to+\infty), highlighting the presence of vanishing or exploding gradients, depending on the regime of the target dynamics.

Proof.

The asymptotic behavior of the gradient in (52), for λ^→±∞\hat{\lambda}\to\pm\infty, is obtained by applying (46) to the closed-form expression of the gradient (49). Considering the infinite-horizon behavior, in the unstable regime λ>0\lambda>0 we distinguish between three cases: (i) for λ^<−λ\hat{\lambda}<-\lambda, both M1​(2​λ^)M_{1}(2\hat{\lambda}) and M1​(λ+λ^)M_{1}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda}) converge to finite values by (47), while M0​(2​λ)M_{0}(2\lambda) at the denominator diverges exponentially fast in TT, hence governing the asymptotic behavior of the gradient towards zero; (ii) for |λ^|<λ|\hat{\lambda}|<\lambda, both terms M1​(2​λ^)/M0​(2​λ)M_{1}(2\hat{\lambda})/M_{0}(2\lambda) and M1​(λ+λ^)/M0​(2​λ)M_{1}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})/M_{0}(2\lambda) converge exponentially fast to zero, with the second term being slower, hence dominating; (iii) for λ^>λ\hat{\lambda}>\lambda, both terms diverge exponentially fast in TT, with the first term, M1​(2​λ^)/M0​(2​λ)M_{1}(2\hat{\lambda})/M_{0}(2\lambda), dominating over the second, M1​(λ+λ^)/M0​(2​λ)M_{1}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})/M_{0}(2\lambda), thus yielding (53). In the stable regime λ<0\lambda<0, it is enough to consider the following two cases: (i) when λ^<0\hat{\lambda}<0 both terms in (49) converge to finite values, yielding the first limit in (54); (ii) while, in the case λ^>0\hat{\lambda}>0, the first term diverges exponentially fast in TT, both in the case in which λ^<−λ\hat{\lambda}<-\lambda, when the second term converges to a finite value, and in the case in which λ^>−λ\hat{\lambda}>-\lambda, when the second term diverges exponentially fast in TT, but at a slower rate than the first term, thus yielding the asymptotic in (54).

∎

The results of Proposition A.1 highlight the presence of vanishing or exploding gradients, depending on the regime of the target dynamics, and how fast such degeneracies occur in the infinite-horizon limit. The behavior of the gradient in the tails of the parameter space, reported in (52), is consistent with flattening of the loss landscape for λ^→−∞\hat{\lambda}\to-\infty, and with the blow-up of the loss landscape for λ^→+∞\hat{\lambda}\to+\infty. In particular, the gradient vanishes polynomially fast for λ^→−∞\hat{\lambda}\to-\infty, while it explodes exponentially fast for λ^→+∞\hat{\lambda}\to+\infty, trivially inheriting the exponential growth of the loss landscape in that regime. In the infinite-horizon limit, the gradient presents a regime-dependent behavior, visualized in Figure 2 over the (λ^,λ)(\hat{\lambda},\lambda)-plane, and summarized as follows. In the unstable regime λ>0\lambda>0, the gradient vanishes as O⁡(e−2​λ​T)O(e^{-2\lambda T}) for λ^<−λ\hat{\lambda}<-\lambda, and as O⁡(T​e(λ^−λ)​T)O(Te^{(\hat{\lambda}-\lambda)T}) for |λ^|<λ|\hat{\lambda}|<\lambda; while, for λ^>λ\hat{\lambda}>\lambda, it explodes at O⁡(T​e2​(λ^−λ)​T)O(Te^{2(\hat{\lambda}-\lambda)T})-rate. Instead, in the stable regime λ<0\lambda<0, the gradient converges to a smooth profile for λ^<0\hat{\lambda}<0, while it explodes at O⁡(T​e2​λ^​T)O(Te^{2\hat{\lambda}T})-rate for λ^>0\hat{\lambda}>0.

Now, we consider the Hessian of the loss landscape. In particular, being the loss not globally convex, the perspective of local convergence for gradient-based optimization is adopted, thus requiring a characterization of the Hessian at the minimizer λ^=λ\hat{\lambda}=\lambda. Besides regularity of the loss, as minimum requirement for local convergence of gradient descent methods, it can be verified that the Hessian (50) is positive definite at the minimizer λ^=λ\hat{\lambda}=\lambda, with

∂λ^2ℓ¯x​(λ)=2​M2​(2​λ)M0​(2​λ)∈(0,2​T2).\partial^{2}_{\hat{\lambda}}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)=\frac{2M_{2}(2\lambda)}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}\in(0,2T^{2}). (55)

The following proposition characterizes the behavior of the Hessian in the infinite-horizon limit, highlighting the presence of ill-conditioning in the unstable regime.

Proof.

The behavior of the Hessian in the infinite-horizon limit is obtained by applying (47) to the Hessian at the minimizer (55). The diverging behavior in the unstable regime λ>0\lambda>0 at a quadratic rate in TT is a direct consequence of the asymptotic behavior of the second-order moment M2​(2​λ)∼T2​e2​λ​T/(2​λ)M_{2}(2\lambda)\sim T^{2}e^{2\lambda T}/(2\lambda). ∎

Implications for gradient-based optimization.

We now turn to the perspective of local convergence of gradient descent, to study the practical implications of the above results on the optimization of the trajectory-based learning objective via first-order methods. Proposition A.2 hints at the increasing sharpness of the loss landscape at the minimizer, with the Hessian diverging at a quadratic rate in TT, thus suggesting that the learning rate and the radius of guaranteed local convergence given by Nesterov [2018, Theorem 1.2.4] shrink with TT. The following arguments formalize such an intuition, quantifying the rates at which such degeneracies develop. Following Nesterov [2018, Section 1.2], the gradient descent update for the energy-normalized trajectory objective (44) reads as

λ^(k+1)=λ^(k)−ηk​∂λ^ℓ¯x​(λ^(k)),\hat{\lambda}^{(k+1)}=\hat{\lambda}^{(k)}-\eta_{k}\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda}^{(k)}),

with ηk\eta_{k} the learning rate at iteration kk. Under suitable regularity assumptions on the loss (e.g. C2C^{2} with Lipschitz-continuous Hessian), local convergence of gradient descent is generally tied to the spectral properties of the Hessian at the minimizer. In particular, letting rk:=|λ^(k)−λ|r_{k}:=|\hat{\lambda}^{(k)}-\lambda| be the distance of the kk-th iterate from the minimizer, we have that requiring convergence of the gradient descent update yields the following inequality

0<rk<r¯:=2​∂λ^2ℓ¯x​(λ)β,0<r_{k}<\bar{r}:=\frac{2\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}^{2}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)}{\beta},

with β\beta the Lipschitz44 4 Here, Lipschitz continuity is intended in a local sense, hence holding in a neighborhood of the minimizer, which is sufficient for the study of local convergence. constant of the Hessian ∂λ^2ℓ¯x​(λ^)\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}^{2}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\hat{\lambda}), and r¯\bar{r} the radius of the ball of attraction of the minimizer. By Proposition A.2, we have that ∂λ^2ℓ¯x​(λ)∼2​T2\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}^{2}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)\sim 2T^{2} in the unstable regime, while β\beta can be bounded below by the value of the third derivative of the loss at the minimizer, leading to

r¯≤4​T2∂λ^3ℓ¯x​(λ)∼4​T26​T3=23​T,T→+∞,\bar{r}\leq\frac{4T^{2}}{\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}^{3}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)}\sim\frac{4T^{2}}{6T^{3}}=\frac{2}{3T},\quad T\to+\infty,

showing that the guaranteed radius shrinks polynomially in TT. In particular, the asymptotic behavior of the third derivative of the loss at the minimizer can be derived by applying (47) to the closed-form expression of the third derivative, which reads as

∂λ^3ℓ¯x​(λ)=2M0​(2​λ)​(4​M3​(2​λ^)−M3​(λ+λ^))|λ^=λ=6​M3​(2​λ)M0​(2​λ)∼6​T3,T→+∞.\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}^{3}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)=\frac{2}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}\left(4M_{3}(2\hat{\lambda})-M_{3}(\lambda+\hat{\lambda})\right)\bigg|_{\hat{\lambda}=\lambda}=\frac{6M_{3}(2\lambda)}{M_{0}(2\lambda)}\sim 6T^{3},\quad T\to+\infty.

Analogously, relying on the optimal choice of the learning rate, we have

ηk=1∂λ^2ℓ¯x​(λ)∼12​T2,T→+∞,\eta_{k}=\frac{1}{\partial_{\hat{\lambda}}^{2}\bar{\ell}_{x}(\lambda)}\sim\frac{1}{2T^{2}},\quad T\to+\infty,

thus showing that the learning rate shrinks polynomially in TT, at a quadratic rate, in the unstable regime. The above considerations highlight the role of the time horizon on the smoothness of the loss landscape, as already observed by Ribeiro et al. [2020], and its implications on the convergence of gradient-based optimization. The analysis, while limited to a one-dimensional linear system, sheds light on the possible challenges that may arise in the context of high-dimensional, nonlinear systems learning via trajectory-based objectives, where the presence of unstable modes may dominate the loss landscape. In particular, the exponential rates at which gradients become uninformative, and the polynomial rates at which the learning rate and the basin of attraction shrink with TT, suggest that casting the learning problem as a minimization of a trajectory-based objective to be addressed via gradient-based optimization may be ill-suited.

    thus yielding x^k​(x0)→x¯\hat{x}_{k}(x_{0})\to\bar{x} as k→+∞k\to+\infty, for every x0∈B⁡(x¯,δ)x_{0}\in B(\bar{x},\delta). Hence, considering that x^k+1​(x0)=ΦΔ​t​(x^k​(x0))\hat{x}_{k+1}(x_{0})=\Phi_{\Delta t}(\hat{x}_{k}(x_{0})), and passing to the limit k→+∞k\to+\infty, we have that x¯=x¯+Δ​t​f^​(x¯)\bar{x}=\bar{x}+{\Delta t}\hat{f}(\bar{x}), by continuity of f^\hat{f}, concluding that: (i) x¯\bar{x} is a fixed point of the one-step map ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t}, and (ii) f^​(x¯)=0\hat{f}(\bar{x})=0, that is, x¯\bar{x} is an equilibrium for the learned dynamics.

    ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t} is a local diffeomorphism. The Jacobian of ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t} reads as ∂xΦΔ​t​(x)=I+Δ​t​∂xf^​(x)\partial_{x}\Phi_{\Delta t}(x)=I+{\Delta t}\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x). With a slight abuse of notation, we denote by |⋅||\cdot| also the operator norm induced by the Euclidean norm, so that |∂xf^​(x)|=sup|v|=1|∂xf^​(x)​v||\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x)|=\sup_{|v|=1}|\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x)v|. With this notation, we have |∂xf^​(x)|≤Lip⁡[f^]|\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x)|\leq\operatorname{Lip}[\hat{f}] at every x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, hence the assumption Δ​t​Lip⁡[f^]<1{\Delta t}\,\operatorname{Lip}[\hat{f}]<1 gives |Δ​t​∂xf^​(x)|<1|{\Delta t}\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x)|<1, implying that ∂xΦΔ​t​(x)\partial_{x}\Phi_{\Delta t}(x) is invertible by the Neumann series. By the inverse function theorem, ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t} is then a local C1C^{1} diffeomorphism at every x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

    Jacobian spectral constraint. We proceed by contradiction, supposing that ρ⁡(I+Δ​t​∂xf^​(x¯))>1\rho(I+{\Delta t}\partial_{x}\hat{f}(\bar{x}))>1, so that the unstable subspace of ∂xΦΔ​t​(x¯)\partial_{x}\Phi_{\Delta t}(\bar{x}) is nontrivial. Note that the initial condition x0x_{0} itself need not belong to ℳcs\mathcal{M}^{\rm cs}, its orbit being unconstrained before time k∗k_{*}. Since k∗k_{*} depends on x0x_{0}, this yields

    B⁡(x¯,δ)⊆⋃k∈ℕΦΔ​t−k​(ℳcs).B(\bar{x},\delta)\ \subseteq\ \bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\Phi_{\Delta t}^{-k}\big(\mathcal{M}^{\rm cs}\big).

    Since ℳcs\mathcal{M}^{\rm cs} has positive codimension <n<n, it has null Lebesgue measure in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and being ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t} a local diffeomorphism by step 2, each preimage ΦΔ​t−k​(ℳcs)\Phi_{\Delta t}^{-k}(\mathcal{M}^{\rm cs}) has null measure as well. So, the countable union of such sets has thus null Lebesgue measure, contradicting the fact that B⁡(x¯,δ)B(\bar{x},\delta) has positive measure. Therefore ρ⁡(I+Δ​t​∂xf^​(x¯))≤1\rho(I+{\Delta t}\partial_{x}\hat{f}(\bar{x}))\leq 1, and since σ⁡(I+Δ​t​∂xf^​(x¯))={1+Δ​t​ν^:ν^∈σ⁡(∂xf^​(x¯))}\sigma(I+{\Delta t}\partial_{x}\hat{f}(\bar{x}))=\{1+{\Delta t}\hat{\nu}:\hat{\nu}\in\sigma(\partial_{x}\hat{f}(\bar{x}))\} by spectral mapping, this reads as σ⁡(∂xf^​(x¯))⊆𝒜¯Δ​t\sigma(\partial_{x}\hat{f}(\bar{x}))\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{\Delta t}.

∎

Remark 4.

While x¯\bar{x} is asymptotically stable for the target dynamics by assumption, and hence Lyapunov stable, the first step of the proof only establishes that it is an attracting fixed point of the one-step map ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t}. Lyapunov stability of the equilibrium x¯\bar{x} for ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t} would yield the result at once by a linearization argument, but it would require a stronger assumption than (9), namely that ∑k≥1ak​(x0)\sum_{k\geq 1}a_{k}(x_{0}) vanish as x0→x¯x_{0}\to\bar{x}, rather than merely be finite for each x0x_{0}. Attraction only constrains the asymptotic behavior of the orbit x^k​(x0)\hat{x}_{k}(x_{0}), which may leave B⁡(x¯,δ)B(\bar{x},\delta) during the transient, before converging. The center-stable manifold theorem circumvents this, being applied to the tail of each converging orbit. Then, local invertibility of the one-step map ΦΔ​t\Phi_{\Delta t} ensures that, whenever ρ⁡(∂xΦΔ​t​(x¯))>1\rho(\partial_{x}\Phi_{\Delta t}(\bar{x}))>1, the set of initial conditions attracted to x¯\bar{x} has null measure, yielding a contradiction with the fact that it contains the ball B⁡(x¯,δ)B(\bar{x},\delta), of positive measure.

B.4 Proof of Theorem 3.8, 3.9

We first provide a result establishing that the Gaussian error linear unit (GELU) activation function is an exponential (1,1)(1,1) partition of unity (PU), defined in Gühring and Raslan [2021, Section 4.1] and required by Gühring and Raslan [2021, Theorem 4.9] to establish approximation rates in Theorem 3.8.

Lemma B.1.

The GELU activation function ϱ⁡(x)=x​Φ​(x)\varrho(x)=x\Phi(x), with Φ\Phi being the standard Gaussian cumulative distribution function, is an exponential (1,1)(1,1)-PU-admissible in the sense of Gühring and Raslan [2021, Definition 4.2], with A=0A=0, B=1B=1, C=2/πC=\sqrt{2/\pi}, D=1/2D=1/2 and R=1R=1.

Proof.

The proof follows by direct verification of the conditions (a)-(d) in Gühring and Raslan [2021, Definition 4.2]. Denote by ϕ=Φ′\phi=\Phi^{\prime} the standard Gaussian probability density function. Then note that

ϱ′​(x)=Φ⁡(x)+x​ϕ​(x),ϱ′′​(x)=(2−x2)​ϕ​(x).\varrho^{\prime}(x)=\Phi(x)+x\phi(x),\qquad\varrho^{\prime\prime}(x)=(2-x^{2})\phi(x). (63)

    ϕ,Φ∈C∞​(ℝ)\phi,\Phi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), so ϱ∈C∞​(ℝ)⊂C1​(ℝ∖[−R,R])\varrho\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})\subset C^{1}(\mathbb{R}\setminus[-R,R]), for every R>0R>0.

  3. (c)

    ϱ′∈W0,∞​(ℝ)=L∞​(ℝ)\varrho^{\prime}\in W^{0,\infty}(\mathbb{R})=L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), by (a).

  4. (d)

    Take A=0A=0, B=1B=1. Then, recalling that 1−Φ⁡(x)≤ϕ⁡(x)/x1-\Phi(x)\leq\phi(x)/x for x>0x>0, we have
