We decompose the error between the true trajectory x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}) and the numerical approximation of the learned one x^k​(x0)\hat{x}_{k}(x_{0}), over the time grid {tk}k=0Nt\{t_{k}\}_{k=0}^{{N_{t}}}, into two terms, by introducing the continuous-time flow map x^​(t,x0)\hat{x}(t,x_{0}) of the learned system, as

sup0≤k≤Nt|x⁡(tk,x0)−x^k​(x0)|\displaystyle\sup_{0\leq k\leq{N_{t}}}|x(t_{k},x_{0})-\hat{x}_{k}(x_{0})| ≤sup0≤k≤Nt|x⁡(tk,x0)−x^​(tk,x0)|+sup0≤k≤Nt|x^​(tk,x0)−x^k​(x0)|,\displaystyle\leq\sup_{0\leq k\leq{N_{t}}}|x(t_{k},x_{0})-\hat{x}(t_{k},x_{0})|+\sup_{0\leq k\leq{N_{t}}}|\hat{x}(t_{k},x_{0})-\hat{x}_{k}(x_{0})|,
≤‖x⁡(⋅,x0)−x^​(⋅,x0)‖L∞​([0,T],ℝn)+C⁡(f^,T)​Δ​tp,\displaystyle\leq\|x(\cdot,x_{0})-\hat{x}(\cdot,x_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}+C(\hat{f},T){\Delta t}^{p},

where the bound over the second term follows from the order of convergence of the RK scheme, with C⁡(f^,T)C(\hat{f},T) a constant depending on the learned velocity field f^\hat{f} and the final time TT. By Theorem 3.8, there exists a deep neural network f^∈𝒩ϱ​(ℝn+1,ℝn)\hat{f}\in\mathcal{N}_{\varrho}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1};\mathbb{R}^{n}) such that supx0∈𝒳0‖x⁡(⋅,x0)−x^​(⋅,x0)‖L∞​([0,T],ℝn)≤ϵ/2\sup_{x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}_{0}}\|x(\cdot,x_{0})-\hat{x}(\cdot,x_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq\epsilon/2. Then, choosing Δ​t∗=(ϵ2​C​(f^,T))1/p{\Delta t}^{*}=\left(\frac{\epsilon}{2C(\hat{f},T)}\right)^{1/p}, the second term is bounded by ϵ/2\epsilon/2 for all Δ​t≤Δ​t∗{\Delta t}\leq{\Delta t}^{*}, yielding the result. ∎

The regularity of f^∈ℱ\hat{f}\in\mathcal{F} gives joint continuity of f^\hat{f} over [0,T]×K[0,T]\times K, thus ensuring that 𝔼τ​[f^k​(τ,x0)]\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[\hat{f}_{k}(\tau;x_{0})] and Varτ⁡[f^k​(τ,x0)]\operatorname{Var}_{\tau}[\hat{f}_{k}(\tau;x_{0})] are well-defined. ∎

Prior to proving Proposition 4.3, we recall the definition of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta (csRK) methods, which generalize ss-stage Runge-Kutta schemes to a continuum of stages, following Hairer [2010] and Tang [2018].

Definition 2 (Continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods).

Let a⁡(γ,σ)a(\gamma,\sigma), b⁡(γ)b(\gamma), and c⁡(γ)c(\gamma) be continuous functions of γ,σ∈[0,1]\gamma,\sigma\in[0,1], with c⁡(γ)=∫01a⁡(γ,σ)​𝑑σc(\gamma)=\int_{0}^{1}a(\gamma,\sigma)d\sigma. The one-step method xk↦xk+1x_{k}\mapsto x_{k+1}, applied to (1), defined by

X⁡(γ)\displaystyle X(\gamma) =xk+Δ​t​∫01a⁡(γ,σ)​f​(tk+c⁡(σ)​Δ​t,X⁡(σ))​𝑑σ,\displaystyle=x_{k}+{\Delta t}\int_{0}^{1}a(\gamma,\sigma)f(t_{k}+c(\sigma){\Delta t},X(\sigma))\,d\sigma, (68)
xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} =xk+Δ​t​∫01b⁡(γ)​f​(tk+c⁡(γ)​Δ​t,X⁡(γ))​𝑑γ,\displaystyle=x_{k}+{\Delta t}\int_{0}^{1}b(\gamma)f(t_{k}+c(\gamma){\Delta t},X(\gamma))\,d\gamma, (69)

is a continuous-stage Runge-Kutta (csRK) method, with continuous-stage variable X⁡(γ)X(\gamma).

Here, the continuous-stage tableau (a⁡(γ,σ),b⁡(γ),c⁡(γ))(a(\gamma,\sigma),b(\gamma),c(\gamma)) generalizes the coefficients (ai​j,bi,ci)(a_{ij},b_{i},c_{i}) of a classical Runge-Kutta method. In the autonomous setting, X⁡(γ)X(\gamma) identifies with the collocation polynomial [Hairer, 2010], yielding the continuous approximation of the solution X⁡(γ)≈x⁡(tk+γ​Δ​t)X(\gamma)\approx x(t_{k}+\gamma{\Delta t}) over the subinterval [tk,tk+1][t_{k},t_{k+1}]. Given the relation (68), the resulting method is implicit.

See 4.3

First, we recall some basic estimates about piecewise linear interpolation, which will be used in the proof of Theorem 4.4.

Lemma C.1 (Chord estimates).

Under assumption 3, for every k=0,…,Nt−1k=0,\dots,{N_{t}}-1, t∈[tk,tk+1]t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}] and x0∈𝒳0x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}_{0}, it holds that

|x⁡(t,x0)−x~​(t,x0)|≤M1​Δ​t2,|vk​(x0)−f⁡(t,x⁡(t,x0))|≤M1​Δ​t,|vk​(x0)|≤M,|x(t,x_{0})-\tilde{x}(t,x_{0})|\leq M_{1}{\Delta t}^{2},\qquad|v_{k}(x_{0})-f(t,x(t,x_{0}))|\leq M_{1}{\Delta t},\qquad|v_{k}(x_{0})|\leq M, (76)

|f⁡(t,x⁡(t,x0))−f⁡(s,x⁡(s,x0))|\displaystyle|f(t,x(t,x_{0}))-f(s,x(s,x_{0}))| ≤∫st|dd​r​f​(r,x⁡(r,x0))|​𝑑r,\displaystyle\leq\int_{s}^{t}\left|\frac{d}{dr}f(r,x(r,x_{0}))\right|dr,

Appendix D Experimental details

This appendix details the experiments of Section 5. Section D.1 describes the benchmark systems and the generation of the datasets, Section D.2 the model architectures, and Section D.3 the training and evaluation procedures. Section D.4 provides additional material supporting our results, including the tables of validation and test errors for ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and partial differential equations (PDEs) benchmarks, together with visualizations of the solutions. All experiments were run on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU with 48GB of memory. The code to reproduce the experiments is available at github.com/farenga/velocity-matching.

D.1 Benchmark systems and datasets

D.1.1 Ordinary differential equations

For each ODE system, training, validation and test trajectories were generated from independently sampled initial conditions, by integrating the true dynamics with the DOP853 scheme [Hairer et al., 2008], with absolute and relative tolerances equal to 10−1210^{-12}, and were observed on a uniform grid of step size Δ​t{\Delta t} over [0,T][0,T]. An additional set of test trajectories, observed with step size 10−410^{-4}, was used for the continuous-time approximation study of Section 5.2. The number of trajectories, the step sizes and the time horizons of each split are reported in Table 1. Note that test trajectories extend over a time horizon twice as long as the training one, so that test errors also measure extrapolation in time.

We report the formulation of the ODE benchmarks below, specifying for each system its governing equations, the parametric configuration, and the distribution ρ0\rho_{0} of the initial conditions.

Euler.

The angular momentum x∈ℝ3x\in\mathbb{R}^{3} of a free rigid body evolves according to a Lie–Poisson system [Marsden and Ratiu, 1999, Hairer, 2010], reading as

x˙=x×I−1​x,I=diag⁡(I1,I2,I3).\dot{x}=x\times\mathrm{I}^{-1}x,\qquad\mathrm{I}=\operatorname{diag}(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3}).

The kinetic energy H⁡(x)=12​x⊤​I−1​xH(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}\mathrm{I}^{-1}x and the Casimir invariant C⁡(x)=|x|2C(x)=|x|^{2} are conserved, so that trajectories lie on the unit sphere in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. We set (I1,I2,I3)=(2,1,2/3)(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3})=(2,1,2/3), and sample the initial conditions uniformly on the unit sphere. Since |x||x| is conserved, the trajectories carry no information on the radial component of the velocity field, the Jacobian error (43) is computed in the tangent directions only, namely as the error between ∂xf⁡(x)​P​(x)\partial_{x}f(x)P(x) and ∂xf^​(x)​P​(x)\partial_{x}\hat{f}(x)P(x), where P⁡(x)=Id−x​x⊤/|x|2P(x)=\operatorname{Id}-xx^{\top}/|x|^{2} is the orthogonal projector onto the tangent space of the sphere at xx.

Stuart–Landau.

The normal form of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation [Perko, 2001] reads as

x˙1=μ​x1−x2+(a​x1−b​x2)​r2,x˙2=x1+μ​x2+(b​x1+a​x2)​r2,r2=x12+x22,\dot{x}_{1}=\mu x_{1}-x_{2}+(ax_{1}-bx_{2})\,r^{2},\qquad\dot{x}_{2}=x_{1}+\mu x_{2}+(bx_{1}+ax_{2})\,r^{2},\qquad r^{2}=x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2},

and, for μ>0\mu>0 and a<0a<0, admits a stable limit cycle of radius −μ/a\sqrt{-\mu/a}. We set (μ,a,b)=(1,−1,1)(\mu,a,b)=(1,-1,1), so that the limit cycle is the unit circle, and sample the initial conditions in polar coordinates, with radius r0∼𝒰⁡[0.2,2]r_{0}\sim\mathcal{U}[0.2,2] and angle θ0∼𝒰⁡[0,2​π]\theta_{0}\sim\mathcal{U}[0,2\pi], so that trajectories approach the limit cycle from both inside and outside.

Active Müller–Brown system.

We consider an active particle of unit mass [Romanczuk et al., 2012], with position x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, subject to the Müller–Brown potential [Müller and Brown, 1979] and to Rayleigh–Helmholtz friction, namely

x¨=−κ∇V(x)+(α−β|x˙|2)x˙,\ddot{x}=-\kappa\nabla V(x)+(\alpha-\beta|\dot{x}|^{2})\dot{x},

where

V⁡(x)=∑i=14Ai​exp⁡{ai​(x1−x¯1,i)2+bi​(x1−x¯1,i)​(x2−x¯2,i)+ci​(x2−x¯2,i)2},V(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{4}A_{i}\exp\left\{a_{i}(x_{1}-\bar{x}_{1,i})^{2}+b_{i}(x_{1}-\bar{x}_{1,i})(x_{2}-\bar{x}_{2,i})+c_{i}(x_{2}-\bar{x}_{2,i})^{2}\right\},

with the standard coefficients of Müller and Brown [1979]. The friction term injects energy at low speed and dissipates it at high speed, and vanishes at the characteristic speed v0=α/βv_{0}=\sqrt{\alpha/\beta}. We set (κ,α,β)=(10−2,0.25,1)(\kappa,\alpha,\beta)=(10^{-2},0.25,1), so that v0=0.5v_{0}=0.5. With this choice, the system is characterized by self-sustained oscillations within each of the two deepest wells of the potential, whereas the intermediate minimum is only visited transiently. Initial positions are sampled uniformly in [−1.5,1.2]×[−0.2,2][-1.5,1.2]\times[-0.2,2], and retained only if V⁡(q0)<0V(q_{0})<0, which keeps each trajectory within its initial well. Initial velocities have magnitude v0v_{0} and a uniformly sampled direction. The resulting velocity field spans several orders of magnitude over the domain.

Lorenz system.

The Lorenz system [Lorenz, 1963] reads as

x˙1=σ⁡(x2−x1),x˙2=x1​(ρ−x3)−x2,x˙3=x1​x2−β​x3,\dot{x}_{1}=\sigma(x_{2}-x_{1}),\qquad\dot{x}_{2}=x_{1}(\rho-x_{3})-x_{2},\qquad\dot{x}_{3}=x_{1}x_{2}-\beta x_{3},

and is considered with the classical parameters (σ,ρ,β)=(10,28,8/3)(\sigma,\rho,\beta)=(10,28,8/3), for which the dynamics is chaotic, with the nontrivial equilibria C±=(±β⁡(ρ−1),±β⁡(ρ−1),ρ−1)C_{\pm}=(\pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho-1)},\pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho-1)},\rho-1) being unstable [Sparrow, 1982]. Initial conditions are drawn from a localized distribution 𝒩⁡(x¯0,10−4​I3)\mathcal{N}(\bar{x}_{0},10^{-4}I_{3}), with x¯0=(−9,−3,34)\bar{x}_{0}=(-9,-3,34), so that the separation induced by the chaotic nature of the system is the only driver of the exploration of the attractor.

D.1.2 Partial differential equations

The considered PDE test cases are posed on a one dimensional domain Ω=[0,LΩ)\Omega=[0,L_{\Omega}), with interval length LΩL_{\Omega} and periodic boundary conditions, and discretized with NhN_{h} equispaced grid points, so that the resulting discretized state is uh∈ℝNhu_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{h}}. Time stepping is performed via Fourier pseudo-spectral, second-order exponential time-differencing Runge–Kutta schemes provided by Koehler et al. [2024]. Initial conditions are random superpositions of kk sine waves, with independent coefficients. Trajectories were generated with a fine time discretization and then subsampled in time for training, while validation and test trajectories were kept at the generation step size.

We report the PDE benchmarks below, specifying for each equation the spatial domain, the parametric configuration, and the distribution of the initial conditions.

Burgers.

We consider the viscous Burgers equation, reading as

∂tu+u​∂xu=ν​∂x2u,\partial_{t}u+u\partial_{x}u=\nu\partial_{x}^{2}u,

with viscosity ν=10−2\nu=10^{-2}, LΩ=1L_{\Omega}=1 and k=2k=2, for which the initial waves develop into viscous fronts that propagate and decay over time.

Fisher–KPP.

We consider the following reaction-diffusion equation

∂tu=ν​∂x2u+r​u​(1−u),\partial_{t}u=\nu\partial_{x}^{2}u+r\,u(1-u),

characterized by a logistic growth term, combined with diffusion. We set the diffusivity ν=10−2\nu=10^{-2} and the reaction rate r=1r=1, on a domain of length LΩ=1L_{\Omega}=1. Initial conditions, with k=5k=5, are clipped to the range [0,1][0,1].

Korteweg–de Vries.

We consider the hyperviscous Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation

∂tu−6u∂xu+∂x3u=−ζ∂x4u,\partial_{t}u-6u\partial_{x}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u=-\zeta\partial_{x}^{4}u,

with hyperviscosity coefficient ζ=10−2\zeta=10^{-2}, on a domain of length LΩ=30L_{\Omega}=30. The initial waves, sampled with k=5k=5, break into solitary waves propagating at speeds depending on their amplitude, while the hyperviscous term damps small scales.

Kuramoto–Sivashinsky.

We consider the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation in conservative form, reading as

∂tu+u​∂xu+∂x2u+∂x4u=0,\partial_{t}u+u\,\partial_{x}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+\partial_{x}^{4}u=0,

on a domain of length LΩ=64L_{\Omega}=64. For this domain length, the anti-diffusive second-order term, which destabilizes large scales, the fourth-order term, which dissipates small scales, and the nonlinear term, which transfers energy between them, together result in spatiotemporal chaos.

D.2 Architectures and normalization

We detail the architectures used to parameterize the learned velocity field in the ODE and PDE settings, together with the adopted normalization strategy.

ODEs.

The learned velocity field is a fully connected network of width 256256 for the active Müller–Brown system, and 6464 for the remaining test cases. Three residual connections are employed, with each residual block being a gated linear unit, in which a GELU branch is modulated by a tanh\tanh gate. The output layer is initialized to zero, so that training starts from the trivial dynamics f^=0\hat{f}=0. Since all systems are autonomous, the network takes the state as its only input.

PDEs.

The learned velocity field is a convolutional residual network acting on the discretized state, as in Stachenfeld et al. [2022]. In particular, a first convolutional layer lifts the state to 6464 channels, which is then followed by a sequence of residual blocks with the same number of channels, and finally by a GELU activation and a convolution projecting back to a single channel. Each residual block is composed of two GELU activations and two convolutions, and, for the Burgers, Fisher–KPP and KdV equations, of a layer normalization over the channels, applied independently at each grid point before each convolution. We use four residual blocks for the Burgers, Fisher–KPP and KdV equations, and eight residual blocks for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation. All convolutions have kernel size 55 and circular padding, consistently with the periodic boundary conditions. The last convolution of each residual block and the output convolution are initialized to zero.

Asymmetric normalization.

The input and the output of the learned velocity field are of different nature, namely states and velocities, and are therefore normalized separately, as also noted by McCabe et al. [2025]. Denoting by (μx,σx)(\mu_{x},\sigma_{x}) the mean and standard deviation of the training states, and by (μv,σv)(\mu_{v},\sigma_{v}) those of the finite difference velocities (x⁡(tk+1)−x⁡(tk))/Δ​t(x(t_{k+1})-x(t_{k}))/{\Delta t} computed on the training trajectories, the learned velocity field f^\hat{f} is parameterized as

f^​(x)=σv⊙f~​((x−μx)⊘σx)+μv,\hat{f}(x)=\sigma_{v}\odot\tilde{f}\big((x-\mu_{x})\oslash\sigma_{x}\big)+\mu_{v},

where f~\tilde{f} is one of the networks described above, and ⊙\odot and ⊘\oslash denote componentwise multiplication and division, respectively. For ODEs the statistics are computed componentwise, while for PDEs, they are computed over the whole discretized solution.

D.3 Training and evaluation

Training.

All models were trained with AdamW [Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019], with weight decay 10−510^{-5} and, for a given system, the same number of iterations for all strategies. For the Euler, Stuart–Landau and Lorenz systems, a constant learning rate η=10−4\eta=10^{-4}, a batch size of 6464, and 2⋅1042\cdot 10^{4} iterations were used. For the active Müller–Brown system, we used a batch size of 128128 and a cosine schedule decaying the learning rate from 10−310^{-3} to 10−610^{-6} over 5⋅1045\cdot 10^{4} iterations. For the PDEs test cases, we used a batch size of 128128 and a cosine learning rate schedule from 10−410^{-4} to 10−710^{-7} over 2⋅1042\cdot 10^{4} iterations for the Burgers and Fisher–KPP equations, 4⋅1044\cdot 10^{4} for the KdV equation, and 10410^{4} for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation. These were preceded by 10310^{3} warm-up iterations, during which the learning rate increased linearly from 10−610^{-6} to 10−410^{-4}. Gradients were clipped to unit norm, except for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

Validation.

Every 100100 iterations, the validation trajectory error (41) was computed by simulating the learned dynamics with RK4, at the prescribed validation step size, over the full validation horizon. For the ODE benchmarks, the velocity and Jacobian errors (42)–(43) were also computed along the validation trajectories, solely to assess their decay during training and to check the implicit Jacobian matching property of VM, and were not used for model selection. For each run, the checkpoint attaining the lowest validation trajectory error was retained for testing. For the chaotic systems, no validation was performed, and the last model checkpoint was retained.

Testing.

Test trajectory errors were computed at the step size of the test data, with the implicit midpoint for the Euler and Stuart–Landau systems, and RK4 for all others. For the continuous-time approximation study, the reference trajectories were obtained from an additional test set generated over a fine discretization, sharing the same time horizon of the training set (Table 1), and then by linearly interpolating onto the inference grid.

D.4 Additional results

Table 3 reports, for the Euler, Stuart–Landau, and active Müller–Brown systems, the validation and test values of the trajectory, velocity, and Jacobian errors (41)–(43), attained by teacher forcing, rollout training with fixed and scheduled shooting lengths L∈{5,10,20,50}L\in\{5,10,20,50\}, alongside VM. Table 4 reports the validation and test trajectory errors (41) for the Burgers, Fisher–KPP, and KdV equations, for the same training strategies. In both tables, the validation errors are evaluated over the training horizon TtrainT_{\mathrm{train}}, and the test errors over the extended horizon Ttest=2​TtrainT_{\mathrm{test}}=2T_{\mathrm{train}}, as reported in Tables 1 and 2. Finally, Figures 11–13 report, for each PDE, the reference solutions for four test initial conditions and the pointwise absolute errors of the solutions learned by VM, TF, and rollout training with L=5L=5, both within and beyond the training horizon.
